contract_plain_english: [PDF pages 14-15; anchors: equations (4.8), (4.10), (4.11), and (4.12)] The recursive-summation error is split into an alpha-only random component M and a limited-random-bit remainder A. Chebyshev plus the cited variance result bounds M by (sum_i |a_i|)sqrt(gamma_{n-1}(u_p^2)/lambda) with probability at least 1-lambda, while A is bounded pathwise by (sum_i |a_i|)[gamma_{n-1}(u_p+u_{p+r})-gamma_{n-1}(u_p)]. For nonzero y, combining the two and dividing by |y| gives Theorem 4.3 exactly.

source_evidence.observation: For a finite-variance random variable X and alpha>0, the paper states a probability of at least 1-1/alpha^2 for remaining within alpha standard deviations of the mean.

The paper defines alpha_k=delta_k-beta_k, states that these variables are mean independent with zero mean, decomposes each accumulated product into an alpha-only product plus B_i, and gives a deterministic magnitude bound on B_i.
The proof uses |alpha_k|<=u_p and |beta_k|<=u_{p+r} to obtain the exact remainder envelope gamma_m(u_p+u_{p+r})-gamma_m(u_p).

source_evidence.anchor: recursive summation representation (4.4) and error definitions (4.5)
source_evidence.observation: The computed recursive sum is represented coefficientwise by products of 1+delta_{k-1}; the exact sum, condition number, gamma function, and delta and beta radii are defined here.
For alpha_j=delta_j-beta_j, the paper rewrites each suffix product as an alpha-only product plus B_i and derives |hat(y)-y|<=|M|+|A|.

source_evidence.anchor: deterministic remainder (4.10), Theorem 4.3 equation (4.11), and centered component bound (4.12)
source_evidence.observation: The page gives a pathwise bound on A, a probability-at-least-1-lambda bound on M based on a variance result and Chebyshev, and combines them into the stated high-probability relative summation-error bound.

statement.algorithm_linkage: [PDF pages 13-15; anchors: recursive algorithm, equation (4.8), and Theorem 4.3] The result concerns left-to-right recursive summation with n-1 SR_{p,r}-rounded additions, analyzed through the alpha-plus-beta decomposition; it does not cover another summation order or algorithm variant.
binders: [PDF page 13; anchor: opening of section 4.1] A vector a in R^n, its exact sum y=sum_{i=1}^n a_i, and the SR_{p,r}-computed recursive sum hat(y) from (4.4).
[PDF page 15; anchor: Theorem 4.3 statement] A confidence parameter lambda quantified after the summation setup, with 0<lambda<1.
[PDF pages 6 and 13; anchors: Definition 2.9 and section 4.1] Precision p and positive integer r, with unit roundoffs u_p=2^(1-p) and u_{p+r}=2^(1-p-r).
conclusions: [PDF page 15; anchor: equation (4.10)] The remainder A=sum_{i=1}^n a_i B_i satisfies the pathwise bound |A|<=sum_{i=1}^n |a_i||B_i|<=(sum_{i=1}^n |a_i|)[gamma_{n-1}(u_p+u_{p+r})-gamma_{n-1}(u_p)].
[PDF page 15; anchor: equation (4.12)] With probability at least 1-lambda, |M|<=(sum_{i=1}^n |a_i|) sqrt(gamma_{n-1}(u_p^2)/lambda).
[PDF page 15; anchor: Theorem 4.3 equation (4.11)] With probability at least 1-lambda, |hat(y)-y|/|y| <= kappa(a)[sqrt(gamma_{n-1}(u_p^2)/lambda)+gamma_{n-1}(u_p+u_{p+r})-gamma_{n-1}(u_p)].
constants_and_indexing: [PDF pages 13-15; anchors: equations (4.4), (4.10), (4.11), and (4.12)] There are n-1 rounded additions, and every gamma term in Theorem 4.3 has index n-1.

[PDF page 15; anchor: equations (4.11) and (4.12)] The stochastic term is sqrt(gamma_{n-1}(u_p^2)/lambda): u_p is squared inside gamma, and the whole gamma value is divided by lambda under the square root.
[PDF page 15; anchor: equations (4.10) and (4.11)] The limited-r remainder is gamma_{n-1}(u_p+u_{p+r})-gamma_{n-1}(u_p).
[PDF page 15; anchor: Theorem 4.3 statement] The success probability is at least 1-lambda for every real lambda with 0<lambda<1.
definitions_and_conventions: [PDF page 13; anchors: equations (4.1)-(4.3)] y=sum_i a_i, kappa(a)=(sum_i |a_i|)/|sum_i a_i|, and gamma_m(u)=(1+u)^m-1.
[PDF page 13; anchor: equation (4.4)] hat(y)=sum_{i=1}^n a_i product_{k=max{i,2}}^n(1+delta_{k-1}).
[PDF pages 11 and 14; anchors: Lemma 3.10 and equation (4.8)] alpha_j=delta_j-beta_j and product_{k=max{i,2}}^n(1+delta_{k-1})=product_{k=max{i,2}}^n(1+alpha_{k-1})+B_i.
[PDF pages 14 and 15; anchors: equation (4.8) and definitions immediately preceding (4.9)] M=sum_{i=1}^n a_i[product_{k=max{i,2}}^n(1+alpha_{k-1})-1], and A=sum_{i=1}^n a_i B_i.
[PDF page 14; anchor: equation (4.8)] The decomposition gives |hat(y)-y|<=|M|+|A|.
error_notions: [PDF page 15; anchor: Theorem 4.3 equation (4.11)] The final result is a high-probability relative forward-error bound for one computed sum hat(y), not a bias or expected-error bound.

[PDF pages 14 and 15; anchors: equation (4.8), equation (4.10), and equation (4.12)] The forward error is separated into a probabilistically controlled alpha-only component M and a remainder A with a deterministic magnitude envelope.
[PDF page 15; anchor: equation (4.12)] The variance-based probability estimate applies to |M|, not directly to |hat(y)-E(hat(y))|.
exceptional_values: [PDF page 8; anchor: zero-result case in Lemma 3.2] If a rounded elementary operation has exact result zero, the inherited convention sets its delta and beta errors to zero.

[PDF page 13; anchors: condition number (4.2) and beta quotient (4.5)] The final relative result is undefined for y=0, and the written beta quotient requires the Lemma 3.2 zero-result convention when a partial exact sum is zero.
[PDF pages 5 and 15; anchors: normalized floating-point model and Theorem 4.3] No explicit treatment of overflow, underflow, subnormal values, infinities, or NaNs is supplied.
higher_order_terms: [PDF page 13; anchor: equation (4.3)] gamma_m(u) is exact: (1+u)^m-1; the paper also records gamma_n(u)=nu+O(u^2) only when nu is much less than 1.
[PDF page 15; anchor: Theorem 4.3 equation (4.11)] No terms are dropped in the theorem: both the square-root gamma term and the full gamma difference are retained.

[PDF page 12; anchor: section 4 introductory asymptotic description] The paper summarizes the resulting scale as proportional to sqrt(n)u_p+n u_{p+r}, but equation (4.11), rather than that asymptotic summary, is the exact claim.
hypotheses: [PDF page 13; anchor: recursive-summation algorithm] hat(s)_1=a_1 and hat(s)_k=SR_{p,r}(hat(s)_{k-1}+a_k) for k=2,...,n, with hat(y)=hat(s)_n.
[PDF pages 11 and 14; anchors: Lemma 3.10 and equation (4.8)] alpha_j=delta_j-beta_j; the alpha_j are mean independent, have mean zero, and are used to decompose each accumulated product.
[PDF pages 12 and 15; anchors: proof of Lemma 3.10 and proof of Theorem 4.3] |alpha_j|<=u_p, while the corresponding beta_j are bounded by u_{p+r}.
[PDF page 15; anchor: proof of Theorem 4.3] The variance-based estimate imported as [11, Lemma 3.1], together with Lemma 2.1, is applied to the alpha-only component M.
implicit_context: [PDF page 15; anchor: proof of Theorem 4.3] The probability is over the SR_{p,r} rounding choices; the remainder estimate is pathwise, so only the M estimate consumes the failure probability lambda.
[PDF pages 11 and 15; anchors: Lemma 3.10 and equation (4.12)] M is the zero-mean-alpha component of the decomposition, not explicitly the same random variable as hat(y)-E(hat(y)).
[PDF page 15; anchor: reference to [11, Lemma 3.1]] The source PDF invokes but does not reproduce the complete statement of the external variance lemma.
[PDF page 13; anchors: equations (4.2) and (4.11)] A nonzero y is logically required by the relative error and condition number, although Theorem 4.3 does not explicitly state y!=0.
norms: [PDF pages 13 and 15; anchors: condition number (4.2) and equations (4.10)-(4.12)] Only scalar absolute values are used; sum_i |a_i| is the coefficient l1 magnitude, and division by |y| converts it to kappa(a).
numerical_model: [PDF page 6; anchor: Definition 2.9 equation (2.6)] SR_{p,r} selects an enclosing precision-p value using a Bernoulli probability derived from the p+r-bit approximation fl_{p+r}(x).
[PDF pages 12 and 13; anchors: proof of Lemma 3.10 and bounds following (4.4)] The random rounding error is controlled at scale u_p, while limited-random-bit effects enter through u_{p+r}.
[PDF page 5; anchor: standard floating-point model (2.4)] The inherited model is normalized binary floating point with relative errors for elementary operations.

undebatable_constraints: [PDF page 15; anchor: Theorem 4.3 equation (4.11)] The conclusion is probabilistic, with success probability at least 1-lambda.
[PDF page 15; anchor: equation (4.12)] The coefficient factor in the M bound is sum_i |a_i|, not |sum_i a_i|.
[PDF page 15; anchor: equation (4.10)] The A bound is pathwise and contributes no additional failure probability.
[PDF pages 11 and 15; anchors: Lemma 3.10 and proof of Theorem 4.3] The alpha errors are assumed mean independent, not fully independent.
[PDF page 15; anchor: equation (4.11)] The entire sum of the stochastic and remainder terms is multiplied by kappa(a).
[PDF page 15; anchor: equation (4.11)] The variance term uses gamma_{n-1}(u_p^2), while the limited-precision term uses both u_p and u_{p+r}; these arguments are not interchangeable.

[PDF pages 14 and 15; anchors: equation (4.8) and equation (4.12)] Equation (4.12) controls the specifically defined M component and must not be restated as a direct concentration inequality around E(hat(y)).
